newsitem.title: RWANDA: Aid officials meet in Rwanda in wake of killings.
newsitem.headline: Aid officials meet in Rwanda in wake of killings.

text.p: Aid officials on Wednesday discussed ways to tighten security in Rwanda after gunmen killed four U.N. human rights monitors in the latest in a wave of attacks.
Heads of U.N. agencies and private aid agencies operating in Rwanda discussed how to respond to the increasing violence, putting at risk their work to help Rwanda rebuild from its 1994 genocide.
There have been eight attacks on expatriates in Rwanda in the last three weeks.

Marie Van Der Elst, a spokeswoman for the U.N. human rights office in Kigali, said the bodies of British and Cambodian monitors killed in the Tuesday ambush were flown back to the capital from the southwest town of Cyangugu late on Tuesday.
The two corpses were taken to the morgue at Kigali Central Hospital while plans were made for them to be flown out.
Two other monitors -- both Rwandans -- were killed with them on a visit in a marked U.N. vehicle to Karengera commune in the southeast, bordering on Zaire.
Their Rwandan driver was wounded in the stomach and died later in hospital during surgery.
Van Der Elst said after the ambush human rights monitors in Cyangugu and the western prefecture of Kibuye were ordered back to Kigali and arrived late on Tuesday and early on Wednesday.
Security fears forced monitors in the northwest provinces of Ruhengeri and Gisenyi back to the capital following the killing in cold blood of three Spanish aid workers on January 18.
A 61-year-old Canadian missionary was killed by a lone gunman on Sunday while he was giving communion at his parish church in a village 20 km (12 miles) north of Ruhengeri.
Claude Dusaidi, an adviser to Vice-President and Defence Minister Major-General Paul Kagame, said he was disgusted "at the actions of these thugs".
"In the meantime I don't think the United Nations should suspend operations in any of these areas," he told Reuters.

"What the United Nations should do to assist us in finding these people and controlling them is to give us (the government) more funds and more help. We need this for security purposes -- radios, communications and fighting equipment," Dusaidi said.
"It would mean we could have more gendarmes, more communal police and be in more places. These people are criminals. I do think they will come back and it could happen again," he said.
U.N. officials said they were investigating the exact circumstances of the ambush and few details were available.
"One thing not mentioned in this story is the people being targeted in this attack were our own (government) ministers who were on a sensibilisation visit to the area," Dusaidi said.

He gave no details. Government ministers tour the country trying to reconcile the Hutu majority and Tutsi minority in the wake of the return from Zaire and Tanzania from November to December last year of more than one million Hutu refugees.
The Hutus fled in 1994 during civil war in fear of reprisals for the three-month mass slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he was "shocked and dismayed" at the killings, which U.N. sources said were particularly brutal. There are 139 U.N. human rights officers in Rwanda.
It was the first loss of life from an attack in the Human Rights Field Operation in Rwanda, which monitors rights abuses.

The U.N. human rights office reported on Friday Hutu death squads were killing Tutsi genocide survivors and witnesses to the slaughter, apparently to stop them denouncing people for the 1994 bloodbath.
